title: What Alternative Assessment Is and Why It Matters
brief: Define alternative assessment using the source's own language: it directly evaluates learners' ability to use the language, whereas paper-and-pencil tests show only knowledge about the language. Walk through the source's five reasons for using alternative assessment (real communicative use, demonstrating actual learning against pre-set criteria, learner involvement in evaluation, increased motivation, and the chance to display progress to family and community). Close by listing the full menu of alternative assessment types named in the source — self-assessment, self-record-keeping, peer feedback, portfolios, performance assessment, observations, conferences/interviews, learning logs, and journals — so learners see the breadth of options before the unit examines each in depth.

title: Self-Record-Keeping and Peer Assessment
brief: Cover the two closely related practices the source treats together. For self-record-keeping, draw on the source's classroom example of wall charts where students track completed reading and homework assignments, noting that these materials need not be expensive and can be made from recycled cardboard or paper. For peer assessment, use the source's description of students working in pairs on a writing assignment: peers can help each other understand the assignment, share ideas for content and organisation, and give feedback on ideas, structure, and clarity — making this a form of formative evaluation. Emphasise the source's condition that pairs must have clear guidelines from the teacher so they know what to look for, and that students bear responsibility for staying on task, completing work within the allotted time, and taking their role as peer evaluator seriously.

title: Portfolios: Building a Record of Progress
brief: Define a portfolio using the source's vocabulary section (a systematic collection of a learner's work over a period of time, evaluated according to pre-set criteria) and expand with the source's four reasons for using portfolios: keeping all work in one place so teachers and students can track progress and identify strengths and gaps; giving students responsibility for tracking their own work and reflecting on their learning; allowing parents, principals, and directors to see progress; and suitability for any age or proficiency level. Use the source's concrete physical examples — younger students using large plastic envelopes kept in bins, older students using large binders kept on classroom shelves — to ground the discussion in practical classroom reality. Note the source's point that students and teacher together typically decide what goes into the portfolio and what the evaluation criteria will be.

title: Performance Assessment and Rubrics
brief: Explain performance assessment using the source's two-part formula: a task to perform plus criteria for a successful performance. During the performance, teacher and student audience evaluate using the established criteria; afterwards they give constructive feedback to the performers. Draw on the source's two video examples — students reporting group research results (using reading, organising, speaking, and writing skills) and a group dramatisation of King Lear (using listening, reading comprehension, reading fluency, pronunciation, and dramatic reading) — to show how varied performance tasks can be. Use the source's list of possible purposes (practising pronunciation, building oral fluency, developing study skills, learning to give oral reports, building confidence, inspiring creativity) to illustrate that criteria should reflect the specific goals of the class, and that the teacher may set criteria alone or negotiate them with students. Connect criteria and guidelines to the source's definition: standards set in advance and shared with the learner that establish how a performance will be evaluated.

title: The Four Defining Characteristics of Alternative Assessment
brief: Synthesise the unit by presenting the source's four characteristics that define any form of alternative assessment: it begins with course objectives; it provides learners with criteria describing successful achievement in advance; it evaluates actual student performance; and the student is part of the evaluation process. Use these characteristics to draw a clear contrast with traditional discrete-point tests, which the source describes as measuring knowledge about the language rather than ability to use it. Discuss when alternative assessment is the stronger choice — when the goal is to evaluate real communicative use, track progress over time, or involve learners in self-direction — and when a more traditional approach may still serve a purpose, drawing only on the source's framing of summative versus formative assessment and the distinction between testing language knowledge and language use.

title: Putting It Into Practice: Designing Your Own Alternative Assessment
brief: Guide learners through the source's four-step action plan. Step 1: choose a language learning objective from their own course and identify which form of alternative assessment fits it. Step 2: design either a short-term lesson task with assessment criteria or a long-term multi-session evaluation plan — both requiring a written set of criteria to determine whether the objective has been achieved. Step 3: share the plan with peers, explain the criteria, and gather feedback. Step 4: revise the design based on feedback before trying it with a class. Reinforce throughout that criteria must be shared with learners in advance, connecting back to the unit's core principle that learners need to know what successful completion looks like — a thread running through every form of alternative assessment covered in the source.
